tip: For frequency Welsh uses 'yr' (the) where English uses a: 'ddwywaith yr wythnos' means twice a week, literally twice the week.
'pa mor' plus an adjective asks how much of a quality: 'pa mor aml' means how often, since 'aml' means frequent.
'cyn' (before) takes the plain verb, never a tensed one: 'cyn mynd allan' means before going out.
Welsh keeps 'mae' (singular is) even with a plural subject: 'mae cychod' means there are boats.
A feminine singular noun usually softens its first sound after 'y' (the): 'pêl' turns into 'y bêl'.
After 'hoffi' (like) use the plain verb for the -ing sense: 'hoffi cerdded' means like walking.
The past tense puts the verb first with the ending on it: 'nofion ni' means we swam, with '-on ni' for we.
An adjective softens after a feminine singular noun: 'coch' becomes 'goch' in 'y ddraig goch'.
Feminine 'ei' (her/its) aspirates the next word: 'traethau' becomes 'a'i thraethau' (and its beaches).
The word 'a' (and) aspirates a following p, t or c: 'persli' becomes 'a phersli'.
'wedi' plus a plain verb makes the perfect tense: 'wedi profi' means have proven.
'caewyd' = was closed. The '-wyd' ending forms an impersonal past, an action with no named doer, like the English passive.
'gwledydd' shows up as 'wledydd' after 'o' (from). The preposition 'o' triggers soft mutation, so the g drops away.
'dewrach' = braver. Add '-ach' to an adjective to build the comparative, the same job the English -er ending does.
'hon' means this and pairs with feminine nouns; here it follows 'dref'. Masculine nouns take 'hwn' instead.
'os bydd y pris yn disgyn' = if the price drops. After 'os' for real conditions, Welsh uses the future 'bydd', not the present.
'cyrhaeddon ni' = we reached. The past-tense we ending is '-on', attached to the stem before 'ni'.
'fy' (my) triggers nasal mutation: 'plentyn' becomes 'mhlentyn', so p turns into mh.
'cloais i' = I locked. The past-tense I ending is '-ais', attached to the stem before 'i'.
'pymtheg' shows up as 'bymtheg' here. The object of a short-form verb like 'cyfrifodd' takes soft mutation.
'cafodd y tŷ ei beintio' = the house was painted, literally got its painting. Welsh builds this passive with 'cael' plus 'ei'.
'ar ôl iddo orffen' = after he finished. Welsh says after to-him finishing, using 'i' with a pronoun ending plus the plain verb.
'mae gen i' = I have, literally it-is with-me. Welsh has no verb to have; it uses the position word 'gan'.
'ei' here means his and triggers soft mutation, so 'brwdfrydedd' becomes 'frwdfrydedd'.
'a' means and, and it triggers aspirate mutation: 'Cymraeg' becomes 'Chymraeg', so c turns into ch.
'coch' appears as 'goch' here. Adjectives soft-mutate after a feminine singular noun like 'ddraig'.
'â' means with in the sense of using or by means of: 'â dail aur' = with golden leaves.
'wedi' marks a completed action: 'wedi blino' = have grown tired. Swap the ongoing 'yn' for 'wedi' to show it is done.
'tra' means while and sets up two things happening at once: 'tra oedd y cogydd...' = while the cook was...
Verbs ending in '-wch' give a command to a group or a polite you: 'ailadroddwch' means repeat, said to more than one person.
